steps.title: Import TypeScript and define state machine types
steps.instruction: Create type definitions for the possible states and transitions of a traffic light state machine. Define a union type 'TrafficLightState' with three possible string literal values: 'red', 'yellow', and 'green'. Then define a type 'TrafficLightTransition' that is an object with 'from' and 'to' properties, both of type 'TrafficLightState'.
steps.hint: Use TypeScript's type keyword to create union types and object types. For the union type, use the pipe (|) operator to combine string literals.
steps.seedCode: // Define your state machine types here
steps.expectedOutcome: You will have two TypeScript type definitions: TrafficLightState (a union of three string literals) and TrafficLightTransition (an object type with from/to properties).
successCriteria: The code defines a TrafficLightState union type with 'red', 'yellow', and 'green' values, and a TrafficLightTransition object type with from and to properties of type TrafficLightState.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Great! You've successfully defined the type foundation for your state machine. These types will ensure type safety as you build the state transitions.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're on the right track, but check that you've defined both types correctly. Make sure TrafficLightState includes all three traffic light colors and TrafficLightTransition has the correct property types.
steps.feedbackWrong: The types aren't defined as requested. Remember to create two separate type definitions using TypeScript's type syntax with the exact names and structures specified.

steps.title: Define the State type using union types
steps.instruction: Create a type named 'State' that represents all possible states as string literals using a union type. The possible states are: 'idle', 'loading', 'success', and 'error'.
steps.hint: Use the 'type' keyword followed by 'State = ' and then list the string literals separated by the pipe (|) symbol.
steps.analogousExample:
// Similar: union type for status
type Status = 'pending' | 'active' | 'inactive';
steps.seedCode: // Define your state machine types here
steps.expectedOutcome: A State type is defined with four possible string literal values.
successCriteria: The code defines a type named 'State' with the union type 'idle' | 'loading' | 'success' | 'error'.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Great! You've successfully defined the State type using a union of string literals. This creates a type-safe way to represent all possible states in your state machine.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're on the right track, but make sure your State type includes all four string literals: 'idle', 'loading', 'success', and 'error'.
steps.feedbackWrong: Let's try again. Create a type named 'State' that is a union of the four string literals: 'idle', 'loading', 'success', and 'error'.

steps.title: Define the Event type using union types
steps.instruction: Create an Event type using TypeScript union types to represent all possible transition events as string literals. Add it after your State type definition.
steps.hint: Use the 'type' keyword followed by Event = and then list your event names as string literals separated by the pipe (|) symbol.
steps.analogousExample:
// Example: defining a union type for events
type Event = 'start' | 'pause' | 'stop' | 'reset';
steps.expectedOutcome: You should have an Event type defined with string literal union values representing possible events.
successCriteria: An Event type is defined using union types with string literals.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Great! You've successfully defined the Event type using union types. This creates a type-safe way to represent all possible events in your state machine.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're on the right track, but make sure your Event type uses union types with string literals (like 'event1' | 'event2').
steps.feedbackWrong: The Event type definition is missing or incorrect. Remember to use the 'type' keyword and union types with string literals.

steps.title: Create the transition table type
steps.instruction: Define a new type called TransitionTable that maps each State to an object describing possible events and their resulting states.
steps.hint: Use a TypeScript Record type where the keys are State values and the values are objects with event-result mappings.
steps.expectedOutcome: A TransitionTable type is defined that provides a type-safe structure for state transitions.
successCriteria: The TransitionTable type is defined using TypeScript's Record utility type or equivalent mapped type syntax.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Great! You've created a type-safe transition table structure that will enforce valid state transitions.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're on the right track, but make sure your TransitionTable type properly maps State keys to event-result objects.
steps.feedbackWrong: The TransitionTable type definition is missing or incorrect. Review how to create mapped types in TypeScript.

steps.title: Initialize the state machine with current state
steps.instruction: Create a variable named 'currentState' and initialize it with the 'idle' state using the State type.
steps.hint: Declare a variable with type annotation and assign it one of the valid states from your State union type.
steps.analogousExample:
// Example: initializing a typed variable
const status: 'pending' | 'completed' = 'pending';
steps.expectedOutcome: A variable named currentState is declared with the State type and initialized to 'idle'.
successCriteria: The currentState variable is declared with explicit State type annotation and initialized with 'idle'.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Great! You've successfully initialized the state machine with a starting state.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're close. Make sure currentState has the State type annotation and is set to 'idle'.
steps.feedbackWrong: Let's try again. Create a variable named currentState with type State = 'idle'.

steps.title: Define the transition function signature
steps.instruction: Define a function type named 'TransitionFunction' that takes a current state and an event as parameters and returns a new state.
steps.hint: Create a type alias for a function signature. Use the State and Event types you defined earlier.
steps.analogousExample:
// Example: a function type for a simple operation
type MathOperation = (a: number, b: number) => number;
steps.expectedOutcome: A 'TransitionFunction' type is added to the code, specifying the signature for transitioning between states.
successCriteria: The 'TransitionFunction' type is defined with parameters for current state and event, and returns a new state.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Great! You've defined a type-safe interface for the transition function. This ensures all transitions follow the same signature.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're on the right track, but make sure your function type uses the State and Event types and returns a State.
steps.feedbackWrong: Let's try again. Define a function type that takes current state and event as parameters and returns a new state.

steps.title: Implement the transition function
steps.instruction: Write the implementation of the transition function that takes currentState and event parameters and returns the next state based on your transition table logic.
steps.hint: Inside the function, use a switch statement or if-else blocks to check the currentState and event, then return the appropriate next state.
steps.expectedOutcome: A complete transition function that handles state changes based on events.
successCriteria: The transition function is implemented with proper logic to return the next state given currentState and event.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Great! Your transition function is correctly implemented with type-safe logic.
steps.feedbackPartial: You've started the function, but make sure it handles all state-event combinations and returns the appropriate next state.
steps.feedbackWrong: The transition function is missing or doesn't follow the expected logic. Review the state machine transitions.

steps.title: Create a simple UI to display current state
steps.instruction: Create a function named displayState that returns a paragraph showing the current state value.
steps.hint: Define a function that returns a JSX paragraph element containing the currentState variable.
steps.expectedOutcome: A function named displayState that returns a paragraph element showing the current state value.
successCriteria: The displayState function is defined and returns a paragraph element containing currentState.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Great! You've created a function that displays the current state value in the UI.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're on the right track. Make sure your function returns a paragraph element with currentState inside it.
steps.feedbackWrong: Try creating a function named displayState that returns a paragraph showing currentState.

steps.title: Add controls to trigger state transitions
steps.instruction: Inside your display function, add three buttons that call the transition function with different events: 'FETCH', 'RESOLVE', and 'REJECT'.
steps.hint: Create button elements with onClick handlers that invoke the transition function with the appropriate event strings.
steps.expectedOutcome: The UI will have three interactive buttons that can trigger state transitions when clicked.
successCriteria: Three button elements are added with onClick handlers that call the transition function with 'FETCH', 'RESOLVE', and 'REJECT' events.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Great! You've successfully added controls to trigger state transitions. Each button will now drive the state machine forward when clicked.
steps.feedbackPartial: You've added some buttons, but make sure you have all three: one for 'FETCH', one for 'RESOLVE', and one for 'REJECT'. Each should call the transition function with the correct event string.
steps.feedbackWrong: The buttons aren't properly configured. You need to add three button elements with onClick handlers that call the transition function with 'FETCH', 'RESOLVE', and 'REJECT' events.

steps.title: Wire controls to update and display state
steps.instruction: Update the displayState function to show the actual currentState variable value instead of the hardcoded 'idle' text.
steps.hint: Replace the hardcoded string 'idle' with the currentState variable inside the paragraph element.
steps.expectedOutcome: The displayState function will show the actual current state value instead of always showing 'idle'.
successCriteria: The paragraph element in displayState function shows the currentState variable value using JSX curly braces.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Great! You've successfully connected the UI to display the actual state value. This is the final step in building your typed state machine transitions.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're on the right track, but make sure you're using the currentState variable inside the JSX curly braces instead of the hardcoded string.
steps.feedbackWrong: Try replacing the hardcoded 'idle' text with the currentState variable inside curly braces in the paragraph element.
